around.headline: Rusted streetlight pole falls, kills man in Bengaluru
around.summary: The Times of India reports a man died when a rusted streetlight pole fell. Avoid standing or parking under visibly corroded poles in wind and rain, and report them to BBMP with a photo and location.

around.headline: Bengaluru family loses Rs 22 lakh to a fake PU board official
around.summary: The Times of India reports the family was cheated by someone posing as a PU board official. Boards don't take money to alter marks or secure seats, so verify any such claim with the board or school directly.

around.headline: Fireball explosion leaves 6 of a family injured in Bengaluru
around.summary: The Times of India reports six members of one family were injured in a fireball explosion. If you smell gas, don't switch on lights or lighters; open windows, shut the regulator and step outside.

around.headline: Overnight rain waterlogs roads; woman takes 3 hours to cover 19 km at peak hour
around.summary: DD News reports waterlogged roads disrupted morning traffic, and NDTV and Hindustan Times carried a commuter's 19 km, 3-hour ordeal. With rain forecast again today, allow extra time and avoid low-lying underpasses.

around.headline: BMTC to introduce onboard occupancy counting in buses
around.summary: Public TV reports BMTC will add a system to count passengers on board. It could eventually help plan frequency on crowded routes, though no rollout date was reported.

around.headline: Form 7 misuse row; mop-up drive may give missed voters another chance in Karnataka SIR
around.summary: The Times of India reports a political row over Form 7 (voter deletion) cases and a possible mop-up drive during the SIR. Check your name on the electoral roll now so you can fix any gap early.

around.headline: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel
around.summary: Al Jazeera reports the G7 plans a large release from reserves to ease prices. Whether it curbs pump prices in India remains unclear, so don't expect immediate relief.

street_smart.title: A caller says he's from the education board and can fix your child's marks or secure a seat, for a fee paid in instalments. Your child's results and admission are on the line. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Times of India, Oct 3: Bengaluru family loses Rs 22 lakh to fake PU board official.
street_smart.situation: The caller knows your child's name and exam details and sounds official. He says the 'window' closes in two days, and asks for a first payment of Rs 1 lakh, then more later.

choices.text: Pay the first instalment to secure the seat and sort out the rest later.
choices.feedback: Scammers start small and keep escalating, each payment justified by the last one (sunk-cost trap). Rs 22 lakh was lost in the reported case. No official can legally sell marks or seats.

choices.text: Stop talking, verify through the board's or college's official office or website, and report to 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.
choices.feedback: Real boards and colleges never take money to change results. Verifying through contact details you find yourself breaks the scammer's urgency and control of the conversation.

choices.text: Ask him to send his ID card photo and a receipt format first, then decide.
choices.feedback: IDs and receipts are easy to forge, and engaging keeps you on his script. Checks must come from a channel he doesn't control.

choices.text: Ask a friend who 'knows someone' to confirm the caller is genuine.
choices.feedback: Word-of-mouth endorsement is how these schemes spread. Scammers often plant names of real-sounding officials, so it isn't verification.

takeaways: No board or college takes cash to change marks or reserve seats; admissions go through official portals only.
If you've paid, call 1930 (cyber fraud helpline) immediately; early reporting helps freeze the money.
Urgency plus secrecy plus 'insider access' is the signature of a fraud, so pause and verify independently.
